message.content:
Let  
\[
p(n)=n^2-n+41.
\]
Then
\[
p(n+1)=(n+1)^2-(n+1)+41=n^2+n+41.
\]

If a common divisor \(d>1\) divides both \(p(n)\) and \(p(n+1)\), then it divides their difference:
\[
p(n+1)-p(n)=(n^2+n+41)-(n^2-n+41)=2n.
\]

Now \(p(n)=n^2-n+41=n(n-1)+41\), which is always odd, so no common divisor can be even. Thus any odd common prime divisor \(q\) divides \(2n\), hence \(q\mid n\). Since \(q\mid p(n)\), we get
\[
p(n)\equiv 41 \pmod q,
\]
so \(q\mid 41\). Therefore the only possible common prime factor is \(41\).

For \(41\) to divide both \(p(n)\) and \(p(n+1)\), we need \(41\mid 2n\), hence \(41\mid n\). The smallest positive such \(n\) is \(41\).

Check:
\[
p(41)=41^2-41+41=41^2,
\]
\[
p(42)=42^2-42+41=1763=41\cdot 43.
\]
They share the common factor \(41\).

The answer is 41.
